newsitem.title: UK: Panamaxes continue to lead BFI higher.
newsitem.headline: Panamaxes continue to lead BFI higher.

text.p: Another impressve display of increasing strength in the Panamax sector pushed the BFI up a further 9 points today to 1063 on Friday.
Brokers said that due to the rising price of bunkers the modern economical Panamaxes included in the BFI timecharter definitions were benefiting most from the current market.
The disparity in timecharter rates between modern and older tonnage was widening again.
Meanwhile Caper conditions remained very poor for owners and certain sections of the Handy-size freight market such as east coast S.America, S.Africa and the far East were still very weak.
GRAIN - Pressure to charter modern Panamaxes in the US Gulf persuaded Toepfer to split or reduce their October heavy grain stem to Poland.

It is believed charterers fixed about 35/40,000 tonnes at $11.25 a couple of days ago with 5,000 discharge and that Cargill have now covered a cargo of 1.5/1.6m cft US Gulf to Continent for prompt loading (also reduced from panamax size) at just below $13.00.
In addition Cargill were understood to have fixed a handy-size meals cargo US Gulf/Melbourne on private terms.

Latest rates for Handy fixtures from the Plate were especially weak. Hanjin booked a 27,000 dwt vessel, possibly Lok Pragati, at an economical $5,700 daily plus $70,000 bonus to load barley from S.Australia to S.Korea.

But Halla covered 52/54,000 heavy grain NoPac/Japan with Fareast Victory for mid Nov at a significantly firmer $11, basis no combo. Hanjin were linked with Full Spring 69,587 dwt for an end Oct/early Nov stem from US Gulf to S.Korea but further details were lacking.
MINERALS - The caper market was still "disastrous" according to one leading broker in the business.

A few unremarkable coal and ore fixtures were seen although full information of reported fixtures of Singapore Ace 133,000 dwt in the Atlantic and Hanjin Capetown for a December shipment of 120,000 coal Richards Bay/Rotterdam have yet to emerge.

Panamaxes were a different story, east and west. Coe and Clerici fixed Invader 64,471 dwt delivery prompt US Gulf for a coal cargo to west Med at a firmer $7,450 daily plus $165,000 bonus and Transfield paid as much as $10,900 daily plus $135,000 bonus for Torm Gerd delivery Morehead City early nov for a fertilizer cargo to China.

Over-age vessels have not enjoyed such buoyant demand and it is understood that private fixtures completed this week in the Atlantic of the 1978-buil Petropolis 60,970 dwt and 1981-built Petra 64,848 dwt were at relatively poor levels.
New York reports a 70,500 dwt vessel was fixed delivery US E.Coast in November for 2-4 months at $6,850 daily plus $65,000 bonus were not confirmed.

In the east the 1983-built Neptune Altair 66,764 dwt was fixed by HMM delivery Nopac Oct/Nov trip far East at $7,350 daily plus $175,000 bonus. By comparison earlier this week the 1989-built Amalia del Bene 64,221 dwt was taken by Noble Nopac/China at only $6,500 daily plus $120,000 bonus.

There are reports that a 1981-built 65,000 dwt vessel has been fixed delivery Taiwan for an Australian round at $7,000 daily and the Merchant Pride 69,458 dwt delivery S.China Oct 15/20 for similar business on subjects at $8,500 daily.
The S.African market continued weak with Sun P fixed on subjects by Cobelfret for 70,000 coal Richards Bay/Le Havre for oct/nov at $6.50.
Reports that Klaveness fixed Panamax tonnage with coal Banjermasin/US Gulf and Cockerill Mobile/Continent could not be verified.

HANDY-SIZES - Far East markets continued to be poor. Following Furness Withy's fixture of a 37,000 dwt craned vessel earlier this week delivery Penang mid Oct trip Continent at $3,950 daily it was said that World Aegeus 37,564 dwt was fixed by Continental Pacific delivery prompt Sabah for a 90/100 day trip to the Continent also at under $4,000 daily.
S.Africa and S.America offer little profitable business for owners. The Continent is barely steady in most handy-sizes although the smaller bulkers and lakers are in healthy demand.
